content: 1. Psychological therapies, such as Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), have been studied in Sweden, with evidence suggesting low to moderate confidence in their effectiveness. 2. Adolescents found psychological interventions like ACT and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) more acceptable when they were given a choice of tasks that suited their personal preferences and when the purpose of the tasks was clear. This was observed in studies conducted in Sweden, the USA, and Canada, with high confidence in the findings. 3. Digital tools, such as the DARWeb and Pain Squad+ smartphone app, were highly acceptable in Spain and Canada for managing pain in adolescents. 4. Adolescents were more likely to use psychological techniques in their daily lives when they perceived positive outcomes from these interventions. This was particularly noted with WebMAP CBT in the USA and Canada, with moderate confidence in the findings. 5. Some children aged 9 years and older, along with their parents, were less likely to engage with interventions if the content did not seem relevant to their needs. This was observed in CBT (WebMAP) and DARWeb interventions in the USA, Canada, and Spain, with moderate confidence. 6. Adolescents with abdominal pain or childhood-onset systemic lupus erythematosus expressed reluctance to use coping skills learned in interventions, such as CBT (AIM & TEACH), in front of their peers. This was noted in the USA with low confidence. 7. Psychological interventions, such as Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) and TEACH, were more acceptable when tailored to the individual child’s developmental and cognitive needs, as well as their physical abilities. Tailoring included adjustments in format (visual or auditory), language complexity, and task difficulty. This was observed in Sweden, the USA, the UK, Australia, and Zambia, with high confidence. 8. Children aged 9 years and older and their parents found that skills learned in psychological interventions were transferable and improved factors such as sleep problems, anxiety, mood, and quality of life. This was noted in CBT, Problem-Solving Skills Training (PSST), DARWeb, pain neuroscience education, AIM/ADAPT, and TEACH interventions in the USA, Spain, and Portugal, with moderate confidence. 9. Children aged 9 years and older perceived that psychological interventions, such as TEACH, DARWeb, and CBT, alleviated pain associated with conditions like neck pain, abdominal pain, lupus, and headaches/migraines. This was observed in the USA, Spain, and Portugal, with low confidence. 10. Group-based delivery of physical and psychological interventions helped normalize chronic pain for children and provided a supportive environment for sharing experiences. However, some children in ACT group sessions felt guilt or impostor syndrome if they perceived their pain as less severe than others. Negative group dynamics, if not addressed by facilitators, could also lead to negative experiences. This was observed in the USA, Canada, Australia, and Sweden, with high confidence. 11. Families often found it burdensome to travel for repeated face-to-face intervention sessions, which acted as a barrier to participation in physical and psychological therapies. This was noted in the USA, Canada, and Australia, with moderate confidence. 12. Competing commitments, such as school, homework, and after-school activities, sometimes interfered with children’s ability to practice skills learned in CBT interventions. This was observed in the USA and Spain, with moderate confidence. 13. Social support, such as assistance from school staff, improved adherence to physical therapy (PT) interventions. Parents of children undergoing WebMAP psychological interventions also expressed a need for ongoing social and booster support after the program ended. This was noted in the USA, Canada, and Australia, with moderate confidence. 14. Repetitive PT exercises prescribed for children aged 7 years and older with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) often led to boredom, adherence problems, and family conflict. This was observed in the UK and Australia, with high confidence. 15. Parents of children over 8 years with JIA reported that their children were reluctant to engage in physical exercises that made them feel different from their peers, reducing opportunities for joint movement and exercise. This was noted in Australia, with low confidence. 16. Both parents and instructors observed improved physical fitness in children with JIA and teenagers with fibromyalgia following group or home-based PT interventions. Teenagers in the FIT Teens program reported decreased pain flares, increased strength, stamina, and physical functioning. This was observed in the USA, Canada, Australia, and Sweden, with high confidence. 17. Improved balance and reduced falls were reported after one PT intervention, which increased children’s confidence in their physical abilities and ability to cope with new situations. This was observed in Sweden and Canada, with moderate confidence. 18. Distraction techniques used during PT interventions were associated with reduced pain intensity. This was noted in the USA and Sweden, with low confidence. 19. Female children with JIA or fibromyalgia aged 7–19 years and their parents reported that PT interventions could exacerbate pain, leading to non-adherence, parental distress, and family conflict. Fear of worsening pain was a significant barrier to adherence. Some children with fibromyalgia reported soreness and exhaustion after sessions. This was observed in the USA, Canada, the UK, Australia, and Sweden, with high confidence. 20. Parents recommended peer-accepted lifestyle activities of less than 30 minutes, mechanisms to track improvements, and exercise adaptations based on the child’s health status to improve adherence to home exercise programs. This was noted in the UK and Australia, with moderate confidence. 21. Some healthcare providers (HCPs) expressed concerns about opioid addiction in children, leading to untreated pain. This was observed in Thailand and Morocco, with low confidence. 22. Parents of children with cancer in Jordan, Cameroon, and Indonesia expressed acceptance of opioid treatments for managing pain, particularly in palliative care settings. Free provision of oral morphine in rural Cameroon was welcomed. This was observed with moderate confidence. 23. Cultural beliefs sometimes acted as barriers to pain management. For example, in Morocco, some families viewed pain as inevitable and to be endured, especially by boys. In Zambia, traditional beliefs attributing illness to witchcraft hindered cooperation with pain management. This was observed in Morocco, Zambia, Thailand, and Tanzania, with moderate confidence. 24. Parents in Indonesia reported difficulty judging their child’s pain unless explicitly communicated. This was observed in Jordan, Morocco, Brazil, and Thailand, with low confidence.
